headlines.article_text: HP partners with blacklisted Huawei for licensing Chinese firm's WiFi tech Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points HP has signed a global licensing agreement for certain WiFi patents from Huawei. The company resolved a patent dispute with Huawei on wireless networks late last year. In this article HPQ HP Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The Huawei booth at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, 2025. Arjun Kharpal | CNBC BEIJING — U.S.-based personal computing and printing firm HP has signed a multi-year global agreement for licensing certain WiFi patents from Chinese telecoms giant Huawei, the companies announced Wednesday. It's a sign of adoption of Huawei's technology outside China, despite the U.S. blacklisting the company in 2019, a move that restricted it from working with American suppliers such as Google. "This is a standard-essential patent license covering Wi‑Fi technology - something used broadly across the industry and routine for companies whose products connect to Wi‑Fi. It is not new, does not represent a broader strategic or commercial relationship, partnership, or collaboration with Huawei," HP said. The deal comes after a patent dispute involving HP, Huawei and other companies that resulted last fall in an agreement allowing the U.S. company to access a pool of 2,000 patents related to wireless network connectivity. Huawei was one of the founding members of the patent pool, called Sisvel WiFi 6. The latest global cross-licensing agreement includes "valuable reciprocal patent rights from HP," Steven Geiszler, who represented Huawei in the negotiations, said in a statement. Texas-based Geiszler was a senior in-house intellectual property lawyer for Huawei for nearly a decade , until he set up his own firm in April with Huawei as his main client. HP is scheduled to release earnings Thursday morning Beijing time. HP was spun-off as a separate firm in 2015 after Hewlett-Packard Company was split into two units. headlines.title: Amazon service Bezos once called 'artificial artificial intelligence' is shutting down
headlines.summary: Mechanical Turk launched in 2005 as a way to farm out tasks that are easy for humans to complete but too challenging for computers.
headlines.article_text: Amazon service that Jeff Bezos called artificial AI is shutting down Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Amazon announced it's shuttering Mechanical Turk, a platform that matches workers with small digital tasks, on Sept. 30. The platform launched in 2005 as a way to farm out tasks that are easy for humans to complete but too challenging for computers. Jeff Bezos previously characterized the service as "artificial artificial intelligence." In this article AMZN Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Amazon logo on brick office building facade with windows, San Francisco, California, Aug. 29, 2025. Smith Collection | Gado | Archive Photos | Getty Images Amazon is soon pulling the plug on its 21-year-old crowdsourced work platform, called Mechanical Turk, the company said Tuesday. "We regularly evaluate our programs, tools and services and make adjustments based on those assessments," a notice posted to the Mechanical Turk, or MTurk, website said. "Following an assessment, we've made the decision to close AWS Mechanical Turk, effective September 30, 2026." Launched in 2005, Mechanical Turk matches legions of workers with simple digital jobs, or "Human Intelligence Tasks," that typically pay out a few cents per task. They include labeling data, transcribing audio or video or answering surveys. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos described the service as "artificial artificial intelligence," as it farmed out tasks that could be easily completed by humans but proved too challenging for computers. The service got its name from the original Mechanical Turk , an 18th century chess-playing robot that was actually controlled by a human chess master. Amazon originally conceived of the idea to assist with labeling reams of data on its sprawling webstore, The New York Times reported. Jeff Bezos attends the Viva Technology show at Parc des Expositions on June 17, 2026 in Paris, France. Chesnot | Getty Images Entertainment | Getty Images The platform at one point served more than 500,000 workers, also referred to as turkers, according to Amazon . But in recent years, MTurk had been "in decline," said Krista Pawloski, a data worker and organizer with Turkopticon, an employee advocacy group for data workers. AI models have advanced rapidly since MTurk first launched, while a growing crop of data startups such as Scale AI, Mercor and Prolific have entered the market to recruit workers to train the models. Amazon also looked to capitalize on the demand for AI training by marketing MTurk as a data annotation source for its SageMaker service. "Workers are available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week," according to an Amazon Web Services webpage . "You typically get the fastest turnaround for your human review tasks and labeling jobs when you use the Amazon Mechanical Turk workforce." Pawloski said Amazon seemed to invest fewer resources into improving MTurk at the same time as more data labeling services arrived, causing many turkers to shift to competing platforms. Representatives from Amazon didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Questions have been raised about the quality of some data generated on the platform. A 2023 study from academic researchers in Switzerland found that up to 46% of Mechanical Turk workers used AI models to complete tasks. Last month, Amazon said it would stop accepting new Mechanical Turk customers, which many workers interpreted as a sign that the service would soon be discontinued. Some insurance and travel companies still depend on MTurk for data workers, and are now scrambling to find alternative platforms, Pawloski said. Pawloski started turking in 2008 while she was on maternity leave for supplemental income, before transitioning to the work full time when she was let go from her job in 2012 to help take care of her son with special needs. In 2019, she started organizing with Turkopticon, which originally focused on Mechanical Turk workers before expanding to include data workers more broadly. Mechanical Turk and other data annotation platforms provide "meaningful income" and flexible hours, similar to other gig jobs such as ride-hail services or Amazon Flex package delivery, with the added benefit of being remote and easily completed using a smartphone, Pawloski said. "There's some people that still pretty much still do it full time," Pawloski said. "They're concerned now."
